title: Learned sepsis groups show different observed hospital mortality in an ICU cohort
summary: K-means clustering of eleven routine first-day measurements grouped 8,817 sepsis records into two clinical patterns. Observed hospital mortality differed between groups and remained associated after statistical adjustment. This is a retrospective cohort relationship, without established biological subtypes, causal treatment effects or validated bedside deployment.
ai_technology: Unsupervised K-means clustering of routine ICU clinical measurements
organization: Wuhan University; Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University

evidence.tested: The source selected 8,817 MIMIC-IV sepsis patients and used eleven expert-selected variables measured during the first ICU day. It compared two-to-eight clusters and selected two using clustering criteria. Hospital mortality was 29.4% in the smaller group versus 8.5% in the larger group; adjusted odds ratio was 2.214, 95% CI 1.780–2.754. Outcome differences are actual cohort observations beyond cluster-separation scores.
evidence.unknown: The groups were derived and compared in the same retrospective single-center database, without external transportability testing. They may reflect severity and clinical heterogeneity rather than distinct biological entities. Missing lactate and oxygenation values required imputation; absent baseline SOFA and unmeasured infection characteristics may bias case definition and associations. No causal therapy-response difference, prospective prediction or operational benefit was shown.
evidence.ai_role: K-means learned multivariable patient groups without using mortality as its clustering target; subsequent outcome analysis linked those learned groups to observed hospital mortality. PCA visualization alone and recovery of known individual severity markers are not the represented result.

source_review.scope: Read actual primary sepsis eligibility, variable selection/imputation, K-means cluster-number selection and adjusted-outcome Methods, group mortality Results and limitations. Supplementary implementation and individual records not independently reconstructed. Exact original article front DOI/title and fresh PubMed primary relationship metadata checked.
